Testing a Validator Directly

No app, no mocked Prisma client — a Zod schema is a plain function call, so testing it is just that.

Lesson 2's unit tests (ticket.service.test.js) needed jest.unstable_mockModule to swap out the real Prisma client before the service under test could even be imported (Figure 2.19) — necessary work, but work all the same, just to isolate one function from the database it talks to. A validator has no such problem: createTicketSchema doesn't import Prisma, doesn't touch a network, doesn't have any dependency to fake out at all. Testing it is nothing more than calling .safeParse(...) and checking the result:

// Figure 3.15: a validator test, no mocking required (tests/unit/ticket.validators.test.js, excerpt)
describe('listTicketsQuerySchema', () => {
  it('fills in defaults for an empty query', () => {
    const result = listTicketsQuerySchema.safeParse({});

    expect(result.success).toBe(true);
    expect(result.data).toEqual({
      sortBy: 'createdAt',
      order: 'desc',
      page: 1,
      pageSize: 10,
    });
  });

  it('rejects a pageSize above the cap', () => {
    const result = listTicketsQuerySchema.safeParse({ pageSize: '500' });

    expect(result.success).toBe(false);
  });
});

These are exactly the kind of "unit tests against services/validators" this project has grown from Lesson 1's very first Jest test onward — cheap to write, fast to run, and precise about what they cover: not "does the GET /tickets endpoint work" (the integration suite's job, further down this topic), but "does this one schema accept and reject exactly what it should," independent of Express, Prisma, or anything else in the app. Worth writing one of these for every schema this project adds, the same habit as the tests already alongside ticket.service.js.
